To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

women who have had breast surgery have an increased risk for at least 10 years, that mammography is better at detecting recurrence than clinical examination and that women prefer follow-up in alternative settings to hospital.
women who have had breast surgery have an increased risk for a new primary cancer and a local recurrence for at least 15 years.

women who have had breast treatment have a higher risk of developing a second primary breast and local recurrence than women in the general population and that follow up in the community is acceptable and feasible but further research is needed.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the follow up of women who have had breast conserving surgery and radiotherapy or mastectomy for early breast cancer, and the role of alternative follow-up to the specialist clinic in primary and secondary health care.
identifying the optimal care pathways for women who have survived breast cancer.
the follow-up of women with early breast cancer, and the options for follow-up in primary care and in specialist settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence that follow up in alternative settings is detrimental to women’s survival and may improve their quality of life and reduce costs to health services.
there is insufficient evidence to support or refute any of the options for follow-up of women who have had early breast cancer.
there is insufficient evidence to support any one follow-up model over another.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women who have been treated for primary breast cancer should receive a long term follow up programme which includes mammography at least annually, with the option of having it in the community.

women with breast cancer have an increasing risk of a new primary breast cancer for 20 years or more, that surveillance mammography is effective and should continue for 20 years and that follow up should continue in the community with access to medical treatment as required.
there is no evidence that follow up in primary care is inferior to follow up in specialist clinics for women with breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evidence base for follow-up is weak.
there is no evidence that routine follow up is beneficial for women with breast cancer.
there are no clear guidelines for the best way to provide follow-up for women who have completed their primary breast cancer treatment.
